This was my first "found phone" type of mystery/horror to play so I was quite intrigued by the concept and mechanics as a whole. It really challenged how well of a snoop you were sometimes. Hilariously, I kept getting all the bad choices that ultimately led me to getting probably the worst ending possible and I wasn't really upset by that. However, there were some aspects that were a bit troubling for me throughout my playthrough. 

The jumpscares were considerably louder than the rest of the game and there are no audio options available. I guess I could understand if that was intentional since the "investigation" periods are very quiet (aside from [spoiler]the random knocks which were genuinely terrifying because I thought they were happening IRL[/spoiler]), but I actually did have fun just snooping through/messing with Anna's phone and texting everyone, so the cheap jumpscares took me out of the game pretty often.

Also, the climax (and the ending as a whole) just didn't totally sit right with me for some reason. Maybe my focus was waning by that point, but with hardly enough exposition to help drive the antagonist's motives, it just felt very out of left field. (Okay, maybe if I hadn't gone into this game ≈99% blind and maybe had also known [spoiler]what a simulacrum was[/spoiler], I would've had a better idea of what I was getting myself into.) With all that being said, I was left feeling underwhelmed and unsatisfied.

At the end of the day, SIMULACRA was [b]just okay[/b]. It's already very cheap in price, but I recommend you buy it during a sale if you're really that interested. I have just a small shred of hope for improvement on the second game.

I really love this game genre, but this specific game wasn't very good in my opinion, for the following reasons:
- Inconsistent plot. The game just makes use of random horror movie tropes, without them making sense in the story.
- Very cringey characters (both due to the bad writing and to the bad acting), ESPECIALLY the two most important characters in the game: the girl you're supposed to find and the ultimate bad guy. That's a real problem, because it makes it very hard to emphatize with the person you're supposed to save, as well as to take the bad guy seriously.
- Random jumpscares make this game feel pretty shallow.
- Very, very often, the choices that are proposed to you seem forced. Basically, you can feel that the game WANTS the story to progress in a specific direction, and doesn't allow you to very simply avoid issues by being reasonable. For example, at some point, you can either tell a very dangerous lie or tell the truth. But if you tell the truth, at no point does the game allow to explain yourself, and therefore the person you told the truth to just reacts badly for no reason. In real life it would have been easy to avoid that issue, but the game doesn't want that. Hence, choices aren't well made, and overall it doesn't feel like you're really making story progress - it actually more feels like you're following the story where it wants you to go.

Still, there also are some good things:
- The phone interface looks pretty realistic, which is at least one immersive thing
- One playthrough is reasonably long (about 4 hours for the first one), especially since the game is very cheap, and there apparently are four different endings. 
- One or two moments in the story were actually pretty interesting, even though they didn't make sense in the grand scheme of things

Overall, I advice against buying this game, as there are many better ones in the same genre; I for example enjoyed Orwell much more, and both its mechanics and thematics are somewhat similar (without the horror movie aspect of it, which is good riddance honestly), but the writing is much better and realistic (and therefore more immersive as well !) and never made me cringe. Still, Simulacra is very cheap, so if you're okay with what I said above, go ahead.

tl;dr if you want a phone snooping game that is better than this (harder puzzles, better writing) + touches on some of the same themes, and don't mind it being non-horror, try out [b]Another Lost Phone: Laura's Story[/b].

I really like the conceit of a fake computer or phone as the setting for a mystery game, which is why a friend recommended I play this. However, I can't say that I would do the same.

The writing is riddled with typos and unnatural grammatical errors. Like, a lot of these characters aren't even convincingly fluent English speakers. (Also the way their only Black character is written is. reductive.) But it does have its moments that feel natural and compelling.

The acting is... bad. They sound like they're reading off a teleprompter one word at a time, rather than speaking a sentence, and the emotional reactions are not convincing. Worst of the bunch is, unfortunately, one of the two guys whose voice you hear the most. [spoiler](By which I mean Greg.)[/spoiler]

The characterization is weird? IDK, you spend most of your time talking to various brands of Men Who Are Creepy To Women, and it keeps asking you to side with at least one of them. [spoiler]By the way, one of them is a registered sex offender. And somehow, that's not even the reason he's creepy![/spoiler] Even your interactions with the women in the cast are usually about various aforementioned creepy men. [spoiler]The closeted lesbian coming out to (she believes) the woman she has a crush on? That conversation fails the Bechdel test, even if you consider the player impersonating Anna to be a "named woman."[/spoiler] So even though it's supposed to be about Anna, it's more accurately about men fighting over a woman-shaped trophy called Anna.
It may seem like I'm kind of harping on this but that's only because so MUCH of their characterization is either behaving inappropriately towards women or being belligerent to people in general. There's not much to go on without that.

As for the narrative, it was... railroady. I didn't feel like I was finding secrets because even if I found out something a little early, one of the guys would just tell me to do it later. The highly telegraphed railroading in the intro was actually my favorite UI moment in the game, but that was a lot more artful than the clumsy dialogue trees that all lead to a single point.
I did think the big bad was interesting, especially the part about [spoiler]how "a strong individual would simulate a better [life]" rather than live fully in a suboptimal one[/spoiler]. Though I felt like that theme of [spoiler]the appearance being more meaningful than the substance[/spoiler], while present in some parts of the game, such as [spoiler]reporting a colleague for harassment being an issue because it could reflect poorly on the company, or the folder of pictures of random women that Taylor just Has, Apparently[/spoiler], was underutilized. Which is odd, because... that's from your villain monologue—you HAVE to establish those themes in the story up to that point.

There's just a lot that could have been considerably better than it was.

TL;DR: Posting this review to help Steam out, since this game does NOT deserve such praise. Honestly, I would have been annoyed but said screw it if it was at "Very Positive"... but overwhelmingly positive? It literally does nothing new, innovative, or even good. In fact, I'd say the only thing it accomplished was copying things done many times before it in an absolutely terrible way. It was a slog to get through from beginning to end. I can honestly say it combined all the crappiest parts of horror movie trailers, the worst creepypastas and a s****y jigsaw puzzle together in a terrible phone-shaped package that lasted for WAY too long. It was 30 minutes of terrible content somehow stretched into 3 hours. In other words, if you get it in a bundle like me, go ahead and stop playing when you decide the moment is right. It's not going to get better.

Got this from the "Overwhelmingly Positive" Humble Bundle. How in the actual f*** is this game "Overwhelmingly Positive" ????? Kids review bomb awesome games on here all the time, and this managed to survive that for so long? I'm legitimately confused and concerned. Did this game get massive press in some media targeted specifically towards children, and somehow avoid literally everyone else? Did the people who hate it just not care enough to leave a review? Again, were on Steam, so how?????

On a particularly boring night, I played the entire damn thing. The first 5 minutes in I already knew it was going to be terrible, but stupidly I played on, hoping for something redeeming to happen to justify the positive reviews and my time wasted. That obviously didn't happen.

Bad writing, bad puzzles, atrocious "scares" (literally all jumps, flashing images and noises, and even then not a single f***ing one even managed a startled shutter from me, with volume annoyingly high), all set to an all-too-overplayed by now "hey, play this game on this device/OS/form of communication" gimmick that I'm frankly by now beyond tired of game developers using as a replacement for an interesting story/plot/writing (Stories Untold is the most recent game to do it RIGHT AFAIK). It was cool like the first 100 times maybe, but I'm over it.

I also want to point out, I don't think I have EVER seen good writing/plot in a game that has characters communicating through a messaging system, then has every character using terrible grammar, punctuation, etc. It bugs the hell out of me.
1.It's usually inconsistent. Some chatacters just spring in and out of it randomly.
2.We're not all 12. Some people actually care about that kind of stuff, so it doesn't make sense to have EVERYONE at some point talking like the slow, overly emotional kid in class.
3.It isn't 1995 anymore. It's one thing to have every character talk like that when they're using AOL Instant Messenger, but for chrissakes, you actually have to make an EFFORT to screw up grammar the way these characters do on a modern cellphone with autocorrect. Ugh.

review_text_raw:
Not the worst but I am surprised at how highly rated this was.
I didn't find it overly scary beyond a few jump scares.  The most believable characters in the game are Anna and her friend, I enjoyed their realistic sideconversations more than most others in this game.  The other 2 main characters were overhammed to the point of ridiculousness which was very jarring altogether.
The game gears and mechanisms running under the phone UI were just a little bit too visible to be believable.  As I found certain conversations softlocked at random points until you hit some other arbitrary checkpoint which unlocked the rest of the thread.  Also some things were just not implemented well.  In what world is a job interview carried out over text?  And every phone call was completely one-sided which was so strange - I don't know why they didn't let you select responses like in the written conversations.
Speaking of dialogue, I didn't feel I had great freedom of choice in responding in conversations - I felt I was always fighting with what I was allowed to say.  And the ending fell rather flat, with a certain character taking a complete 180 degree change in attitude and outlook just so the ending could be tied off in a semi-neat bow.
I do have the second game in the series as I got it in a bundle, and the game wasn't so awful as to put me off trying it, so I will see if these devs have taken on board lessons learned and improved things in the second go round, but this game as it stands I would not recommend it.

The story was nothing if not cliché. The concept of a found phone game is cool, or perhaps was at the time of release, but everything else surrounding this concept left me quite underwhelmed.

So many of the characters are creeps, and I find out I got the bad ending for not helping out either of the creeps continue their creep life.
This game also falls into the pitfall of any visual novel type game, it feels stricly linear and there doesn't feel like theres much you can do to change the outcome of the game. Of course this isn't entirely true; there are mutliple endings. But the steps you have to take to get the endings are either vague or require you to work with the aforementioned creeps to save a woman who shouldn't be placed in these creeps crosshairs.

Also what's the message of this game, that putting on an online persona is bad? Sure, maybe, but we see one character using a persona to her benefit?
Is it that forming relationships online is bad? Sure, they can be. But again; there are benefits to forming relationships online too.

The main villian of the game, if you could call it that, doesn't really have a solid theme. Is it AI? Something paranormal? Eldritch horror? A mix of them all plus more?
Even with this in mind, why make it a supernatural entity? Why can't the villian just be a normal guy, like what happens in real life. It feels like meta commentary for meta commentary sake. 

This is the kind of game I suspect would do well in a youtuber letsplay, it's something to be watched and commentated on. I suspect this because I only really had fun with this game because I was playing it with my friends.

As for the "horror" aspect, its a bit of a joke. Loud noises or random unexpected noises playing at random times - most egregiously "door knocking sfx"

Wouldn't reccomend, but its cheap so do as you will.

My first impression from the game was very good - creepy glitchy visuals here and there, atmospheric sound effect, possibility of creeping into strangers phone (yeah I am stalker af so whatttt) and putting random pieces of information together to uncover the story. Awesome, I love games like this!

As the game progresses, your paranoia is fed more unnerving facts. This guy acts weird, right? Do you really trust him? Isn't he actually psycho rapist? And what about the other guy? What are his plans?

If it would stop there, it would be so good, but the story is unfortunately ruined by terrible, unsatisfying conclusion, and all that build-up atmosphere just vanishes and you stare at the screen like "are you kidding me Mr. Developer couldn't you think of something even cheesier" and you can't help but think about your high school essays where you couldn't think of proper ending of a story so you just shoved some aliens in there and hoped nobody would care.

Anyway the premise and execution are still quite good and I am fully aware that my opinion of the story can be just my personal preference.

I enjoy these 'immersive sim' games where you look through devices for clues to a mystery like A Normal Lost Phone or even Hypnospace Outlaw. I liked trawling through old messages and finding tidbits of information that would help me solve a mystery or hack into a passworded account to find more clues. 

I thought that Simulacra would be similar to those kinds of games, but maybe with a more harrowing twist as it's labelled as 'horror'. However I found there to be minimal 'puzzle' elements here, and any that did exist were fairly obvious to figure out. Instead the game is pushed forward by the other characters in the game, who clearly tell you what to do next at each stage.

So the focus of the game is mainly on the story, which I felt was pretty weak. The characters kept railroading me into doing things I didn't want to, like investigating a topic I didn't think had merit, or making me give information to somebody I didn't trust in order to push the plot forward. I thought the final reveal was bizarre and the 'villain's' motives were contrived. It seemed like the devs were trying to send some fancy message about society but hadn't done a good enough job of fleshing it out throughout the game so it all just felt flat at the end.

Several of the other reviews describe the tone of the plot as 'goofy', which I think is fitting but weird for a so-called horror game. review_text_raw: This game had a slate of good ideas executed poorly. review_text_raw:
The Good Stuff:

The layout and idea behind the game is pretty cool. I like how each "app" generally feels like a real app where you can do whatever, like comment of peoples posts or call random numbers. It is really neat design idea and it is well executed.

I also enjoyed a few of the more difficult puzzles, as they really added a sense of immersion into digging through someone's phone. The puzzles are mainly pretty easy, but the game doesn't baby you through them at all, so you feel smart when you manage to pull of something a bit more complicated.

The Bad Stuff:

For me, story is one of the most important parts of a game like this, and unfortunately SIMULACRA fails to deliver a good one.

Mild Spoilers: [spoiler]While the ending tried to be Black Mirror-esque, I feel like the story fails to properly set up the ending, so it kinda comes out of nowhere. Also, many things in the story aren't well explained or left to Deus Ex Machina[/spoiler]

There are multiple endings, and you will get an idea of what they all are when you finish the game. Some of the potential outcomes have me slightly curious, but not enough to replay it to see them. Perhaps the story would have been more interesting had I gotten a different ending.

I am not a huge fan of horror, but I have played games like Prey and Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice that have a creepy horror feel. The creepiness of SIMULACRA lasts only about the first 30 mins and then you become generally innoculated.

The main title song was also pretty cheesy.

As many other reviews have pointed out, some of the voice acting is on the level of "so bad it's hilarious".

I understand that with a smaller scale game like this it is difficult, but I felt like the chat options often strong-armed me into things I didn't want to say, which made things like [spoiler]gaining Taylor's trust[/spoiler] feel unfair.

The Bottom Line: If you want a game with a good story, there are better games. If you want a game where choices matter, there are better games. If you want a horror game, there are better games. If you just want to see a cool mechanic in action, then you might want to check it out.

===[Additional Comments]===
The voice acting is terrible and feels very performative, rather than being believable phone calls/voice messages. The story is linear, and there isn't much room for creativity (e.g. sending people random pictures to see how they respond), and there aren't really any things to mess around with on the phone that are interesting. The puzzles are ridiculously simple and serve no purpose other than to slow down the narrative. The jump scares, if you consider them that, are pretty pointless and don't enhance the story or experience whatsoever. The writing is generally bad and unbelievable (e.g. [spoiler]the CEO of Phresh Ideas divulging way too much information [/spoiler]), and many of the dialog options do not make sense at all. The characters frequently go between texting and calling in a way that doesn't feel believable, and behave very strangely (e.g. [spoiler]at the end of the game, a character is literally texting you as he's pushing someone to their death off of a balcony [/spoiler]). After finishing the game you can go back through more quickly to see the alternate endings, but it still takes too long, and you still have to sit through a lot of dialogue at the end at the normal speed.

Ultimately I would not recommend purchasing this game, solely because the primary focus of this game is the narrative and it felt weak. I received this game from a bundle.
